An attacker can exploit this by injecting maliciously crafted SQL or OS-level commands into parameters passed from an external entry point, thereby executing arbitrary actions (data theft, privilege escalation).

### 2. Memory Safety [Buffer Overflow] (CWE-120)
**Severity:** HIGH  
**Affected Code:**

#### Attack Vector

### 3. Input Validation [Path Traversal] (CWE-22)

### 4. Concurrency Issues [Race Conditions] (CWE-362)

# Remediation Plan

### Solution Proposals and Code Examples

#### A. Preventing SQL/Command Injection
Use prepared statements instead of dynamic string concatenation for constructing SQL queries. Ensure all potential command-line arguments undergo strict filtering before execution.
```cpp
// Prefer Prepared Statements
sqlite3_stmt *stmt;
const char* sql = "SELECT id FROM users WHERE username=?";
sqlite3_prepare_v2(db, sql, -1, &stmt, NULL);
sqlite3_bind_text(stmt, 1, username.c_str(), -1, SQLITE_STATIC);
```

#### B. Mitigating Buffer Overflows
Utilize modern safer string-handling libraries; avoid legacy functions prone to buffer overrun errors (like gets() etc.).
```cpp
#include <string>
std::getline(std::cin, line); // Safer than cin.getline()
```

#### C. Addressing Path Traversal Risks
Implement whitelists restricting valid filenames/path components permissible within each entry point context.
```cpp
if (!isValidInput(pathComponent)) {
    return HTTP_BAD_REQUEST;
}
```

#### D. Handling Race Conditions
Synchronize accesses properly through mutexes/semaphores ensuring safe multithreaded updates.
```cpp
mutex.lock();
updateSharedState();
mutex.unlock();
```
